summary_zh: 學會在一對一面談中具體、不傷人地給回饋，並用四種完成式把「到現在」和「到過去某個時間點」的事說清楚。

vocab.definition: helpful and intended to improve something
vocab.example: Thanks for the constructive comments on my draft.
vocab.example_zh: 謝謝你對我的草稿提出有建設性的意見。

vocab.definition: to seem to have a particular quality to other people
vocab.example: I didn't mean it that way, but my email may have come across as rude.
vocab.example_zh: 我不是那個意思，但我的 email 可能給人很沒禮貌的感覺。

vocab.definition: something about yourself or a situation that you do not notice
vocab.example: Ask a colleague you trust to point out your blind spots.
vocab.example_zh: 請一位你信任的同事指出你的盲點。

vocab.zh: 把（意見）聽進去並採納（偏英式說法，美國職場也聽得懂）
vocab.definition: to listen to advice or criticism and act on it
vocab.example: I'll take your comments on board when I revise the plan.
vocab.example_zh: 我修改計畫時會把你的意見納入考量。

vocab.zh: 偷工減料；省略該做的步驟
vocab.definition: to do something quickly or cheaply by skipping important steps
vocab.example: We can't cut corners on security testing.
vocab.example_zh: 資安測試不能偷工減料。

vocab.zh: 挺身而出；承擔更多責任
vocab.definition: to take on more responsibility, especially when it is needed
vocab.example: When our lead was out sick, Amy stepped up and ran the meeting.
vocab.example_zh: 我們的組長請病假時，Amy 挺身而出主持了會議。

vocab.definition: when you think about something after it has happened
vocab.example: In hindsight, we should have tested the app on older phones.
vocab.example_zh: 事後回想，我們應該要在舊手機上測試這個 app。

vocab.zh: 遇到某類問題第一個會找的人
vocab.definition: the person everyone asks for help with a particular thing
vocab.example: Kevin is our go-to person for anything to do with Excel.
vocab.example_zh: 跟 Excel 有關的事，大家第一個都找 Kevin。

reading.title: What I Learned from Giving Bad Feedback
paragraphs: Two years ago, I gave my first piece of feedback as a team lead, and it went badly. Our team had been working on a billing feature for three months, and one engineer, Marcus, had missed two deadlines in a row. I told him, in front of everyone, that his code was "sloppy." I thought I was being honest. In hindsight, I was just being harsh.

Marcus didn't argue, but he stopped speaking up in meetings. By the time I realized what had happened, he had already started looking for another job. A senior colleague pointed out my blind spot: I tended to come across as someone who only noticed mistakes, never effort.

Since then, I've changed how I give feedback. First, I do it in private, usually in a one-on-one. Second, I keep it constructive: I describe one specific situation, explain its impact, and suggest one thing to try next time. Instead of "your code is sloppy," I might say, "The last two releases had bugs that we caught late. Why don't we add a test checklist before each review?"

I also ask for feedback myself. Last quarter, my team told me that my estimates were too optimistic, which is why we kept carrying over unfinished work from one sprint to the next. I took that on board, and we've cut our sprint goals by about 20% since then.

The results have been clear. Nobody on the team has cut corners to hit an unrealistic date, and two quieter engineers have stepped up to lead their own features. As for Marcus, he stayed after all. He's now our go-to person for anything related to billing.

questions.q: Why did Marcus stop speaking up in meetings?
options: He was too busy looking for a new job.
The writer had criticized him harshly in front of the team.
His colleagues had stopped listening to him.
He had been moved to a different team.
questions.explain_zh: 第 1 段說作者「in front of everyone」說他的程式碼 sloppy，第 2 段接著說 Marcus 之後就不在會議發言了。找工作是後來的結果，不是原因。

questions.q: What did the team change after the writer received feedback?
options: They hired more engineers.
They set smaller sprint goals.
They stopped having one-on-ones.
They added an extra review meeting.
questions.explain_zh: 第 4 段：「we've cut our sprint goals by about 20% since then」，也就是把每個 sprint 的目標訂小一點。

questions.q: What does the last paragraph suggest about the writer's new approach?
options: It made the team slower.
It helped people feel safe enough to take on more responsibility.
It was the reason Marcus finally left.
It only worked for the senior engineers.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。最後一段說比較安靜的工程師 have stepped up 去帶自己的功能，而 Marcus 也留下來了，可以推知新的回饋方式讓大家更敢承擔責任。

grammar.point: Past perfect for the earlier past
grammar.point_zh: 過去完成式：比過去某個時間點更早發生的事

guide.key_zh: 基準點是現在用 have/has、是過去某時用 had；講結果數量用 p.p.，講持續過程用 been + V-ing

uses.label_zh: 到現在為止的結果、數量
uses.signal: so far, already, yet, ever, never
uses.note_zh: have gone = 去了、人還沒回來

uses.label_zh: 從過去一直做到現在（還在做）
uses.note_zh: have been going = 最近一直常去

uses.label_zh: 在過去某個時間點之前已經完成
uses.signal: by the time…, when I joined, already

uses.label_zh: 到過去某個時間點之前一直在做

mistakes.why_zh: been 後面接過去分詞是被動；講數量或結果用 have + p.p. 就好

mistakes.wrong: When I joined, the team already worked on it for a year.
mistakes.right: When I joined, the team had already been working on it for a year.
mistakes.why_zh: 比「我加入」更早開始、一直持續到那時，要用 had been + V-ing

mistakes.wrong: Where's Ethan? He has been going to the client's office.
mistakes.right: Where's Ethan? He has gone to the client's office.
mistakes.why_zh: 人去了還沒回來用 has gone；has been going 是「最近常常去」

timeline.label: They had been building it for six weeks.
By launch day, they had fixed every known bug.
We've been working on version 2 since June.
We've fixed twelve bugs so far.

examples.en: We've fixed twelve bugs since the beta.
examples.zh: 測試版推出以來，我們已經修好十二個 bug。

examples.en: I've been working on this report since nine, and I'm still not done.
examples.zh: 我從九點就在寫這份報告，到現在還沒寫完。

examples.en: When I joined in March, the team had already launched the beta.
examples.zh: 我三月加入的時候，團隊已經推出測試版了。

examples.en: Marcus was exhausted because he'd been fixing bugs all weekend.
examples.zh: Marcus 累壞了，因為他整個週末都在修 bug。

exercises.q: When I got to the meeting, the client ___ (already / leave).
exercises.explain_zh: 基準點是過去（我到會議的時候），客戶離開發生在更早之前 → had + p.p.。

exercises.q: Ethan ___ (work) on the export feature since 9 a.m., and he's still at it.
exercises.explain_zh: since 9 a.m. 加上 still at it（現在還在做）→ 現在完成進行式 has been + V-ing。主詞 Ethan 是單數，用 has。

exercises.q: By the time Priya found out on Thursday, Ethan ___ (already / promise) the client a new date.
exercises.explain_zh: 基準點是過去（Priya 週四發現的時候），答應新日期發生在更早之前，而且已經完成 → had + p.p.。

exercises.q: By the end of last week, Legal ___ (review) only two of the five contracts.
exercises.explain_zh: 基準點是過去（上週結束時），在那之前完成的數量 → had + p.p.。

exercises.q: Ethan was exhausted on Thursday because he ___ (work) on the feature all night.
exercises.explain_zh: 基準點是過去（週四很累），在那之前「整晚一直在做」→ had been + V-ing，強調持續的過程。had worked 文法上也對，但 all night 強調持續過程，用 had been working 最自然。

exercises.q: "Where's Priya?" "She ___ to the client's office, so she won't be back until three."
options: has gone
has been going
had been going
goes
exercises.explain_zh: 人已經去了、現在不在 → has gone。has been going 是「最近常常去」，不能說明她現在不在；goes 是習慣，也不對。

review.point: Making suggestions: Why don't we… / I'd suggest that…
review.point_zh: 提出建議：Why don't we… / I'd suggest that…

exercises.q: I'd suggest that we ___ (move) the demo to Friday.
exercises.explain_zh: suggest that 後面的子句用原形動詞（move），不要寫 moves 或 to move。

exercises.q: Which question is a natural suggestion?
options: Why don't we ask the client for one more week?
Why we don't ask the client for one more week?
Why not we ask the client for one more week?
Why don't ask we the client for one more week?
exercises.explain_zh: 提出建議的固定語序是 Why don't we + 原形動詞。Why not 後面直接接原形動詞（Why not ask…?），不加 we。

exercises.q: I'd suggest ___ (check) with the team before we give the client a date.
exercises.explain_zh: suggest 後面直接接動作時用 V-ing（I'd suggest checking…），不能用 to check。

guide.key_zh: Why don't we…? 是友善的提議，不是在問為什麼；正式一點用 I'd suggest…

uses.label_zh: 口語、友善的提議：我們要不要…？

uses.note_zh: 美式與正式英文：that 後面用原形，主詞是第三人稱也不加 s（英式常說 should + 原形）

uses.label_zh: 比較正式：建議做某件事

mistakes.wrong: I suggest you to send it.
mistakes.why_zh: suggest 後面不接「人 + to V」

mistakes.wrong: Why we don't ask the team?
mistakes.right: Why don't we ask the team?
mistakes.why_zh: 這是問句，don't 要放在 we 前面

listening.title: A One-on-One After the Launch

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Thanks for making time, Ethan. How's your back? I heard it flared up again last week.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Ethan
lines.text: It's better, thanks. I've been taking over-the-counter painkillers, and I've started using a standing desk.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Good. So, about the launch. Overall, you've done great work this quarter. You've fixed twelve bugs since the beta, and the client noticed.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Ethan
lines.text: Thanks. But I'm guessing there's a "but" coming.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Priya
lines.text: A small one. On Thursday, the client asked why the export feature wasn't ready. By the time I found out, you'd already promised them a new date without checking with the team.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Ethan
lines.text: Yeah, in hindsight, that wasn't great. I'd been working on it all night, and I just wanted to give them an answer.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Priya
lines.text: I get that. But it came across as a bit last-minute, as if we hadn't planned anything. Why don't we agree that any new date goes through me first?

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Ethan
lines.text: That's fair. I'll take that on board. Should I email the client today?

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Let's do it together tomorrow. And one more thing: two new engineers are joining the team next month. I'd like you to step up and mentor them.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Ethan
lines.text: Really? I'd love that. I've never mentored anyone before, though.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Priya
lines.text: You'll be fine. You've become the go-to person for the export code, so you're the obvious choice.

questions.q: What had Ethan done before Priya found out about the problem?
options: He had promised the client a new date.
He had finished the export feature.
He had emailed Priya about the delay.
He had asked the team for help.
questions.explain_zh: Priya 說：「By the time I found out, you'd already promised them a new date」，在她知道之前 Ethan 已經答應客戶新日期。

questions.q: What does Priya ask Ethan to do from now on?
options: Email the client every day.
Check any new dates with her first.
Stop working late at night.
Train the whole team.
questions.explain_zh: Priya 提議：「any new date goes through me first」，以後任何新日期都要先經過她。

questions.q: How does Priya most likely feel about Ethan's work overall?
options: Disappointed
Generally pleased
Worried that he will quit
Unsure about his technical skills
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。她說 you've done great work this quarter，還請他帶新人，說他是 obvious choice，可見整體很滿意，只是提醒一個小問題。

dictation: You've fixed twelve bugs since the beta, and the client noticed.
I've never mentored anyone before, though.
Why don't we agree that any new date goes through me first?

shadowing: You've fixed twelve bugs since the beta.
I'd been working on it all night.
I've never mentored anyone before, though.
Why don't we agree that any new date goes through me first?

prompts.question: Tell your manager one thing you've finished this week. Use one sentence that starts with I've or So far.
prompts.question_zh: 用一句話告訴主管你這週已經完成的一件事，用 I've 或 So far 開頭（打字或小聲說都可以）。
prompts.sample: So far this week, I've finished the first draft of the client report.

prompts.question: A teammate has been giving clients new dates without asking you. Make one polite suggestion in one or two sentences.
prompts.question_zh: 有位同事最近一直沒問你就給客戶新的日期。用一兩句話禮貌地提出建議。
prompts.sample: I know you've been under a lot of pressure. Why don't we check any new dates with the team first?

writing.task: A teammate, Jenny, led a client presentation on Friday. Write her a short email of 80-150 words with constructive feedback. Use three short parts: (1) one thing she has done well so far, with a specific detail; (2) one situation that didn't go well, and what had already happened by then; (3) one suggestion for next time.
writing.task_zh: 同事 Jenny 週五主持了客戶簡報。寫一封 80–150 個英文字的短 email 給她有建設性的回饋，分三部分：(1) 她到目前為止做得好的一件事，附具體細節；(2) 一個不太順的狀況，以及那時已經發生了什麼；(3) 下次可以怎麼做的一個建議。
writing.sample:
Hi Jenny,

Thanks for leading Friday's client presentation. You've done a great job on this project so far. The client has already approved two of our three designs, and your slides were clear and well organized.

One small thing to think about for next time. By the time the client asked about the budget, we had already used up most of the hour, so your answer may have come across as rushed. It wasn't your fault, but it left them with questions.

Why don't we do a quick run-through together before the next meeting? We could time each section and leave ten minutes for questions at the end.

Great work overall, and thanks again.

Best,
Ethan
checklist_zh: 第一段有具體的成果或數字（用 have/has + p.p.）
第二段用 had already 說明「那時已經發生的事」
建議用 Why don't we… 提出，只提一件事
語氣友善：先肯定、再提一個具體狀況、最後給建議

translation.zh: 自從我們推出新的定價頁以來，註冊人數已經成長了 18%。
translation.en: Sign-ups have grown by 18% since we launched the new pricing page.
alt: Since we launched the new pricing page, sign-ups have grown by 18%.

translation.zh: 自從上週推出測試版以來，團隊已經修好了十二個 bug。
translation.en: The team has fixed twelve bugs since we launched the beta last week.
alt: We've fixed twelve bugs since we launched the beta last week.

translation.zh: 我加入公司的時候，他們已經在這個專案上做了一年了。
translation.en: When I joined the company, they had been working on this project for a year.
alt: When I joined the company, they had already been working on this project for a year.

translation.zh: 我們推出新的定價頁之前，註冊人數已經連續三個月下滑了。
translation.en: Sign-ups had been falling for three months before we launched the new pricing page.
alt: Before we launched the new pricing page, sign-ups had been falling for three months.
Sign-ups had been dropping for three months before we launched the new pricing page.

replies.zh: 今天的文法改教過去完成式，用四格對照圖把 have worked／have been working／had worked／had been working 一次排開（基準點是現在或過去、講結果還是過程）；錯誤示範第 3 句和文法第 6 題專門對比 have gone 和 have been going。

reading.title: Giving Feedback to the Boss
paragraphs: Most advice about feedback assumes it flows downhill, from managers to their teams. But some of the most useful feedback I've ever given went the other way. Last spring, our director, Helen, had been pushing us to hit a launch date that everyone privately thought was unrealistic. Nobody wanted to be the one to say so, and morale was quietly slipping.

I'd been putting off the conversation for weeks when a teammate finally nudged me. "If you don't raise it," she said, "we'll all be stuck cleaning up the mess in June." So I asked Helen for fifteen minutes and went in with three things: a specific example, the data behind it, and a proposal.

The example was a sprint in which we had shipped on time only by skipping half of our usual testing. The data showed that bug reports had doubled in the month that followed. The proposal was modest: push the launch back three weeks and use the time to rebuild our test coverage.

What surprised me was not that Helen agreed, but how she reacted. Rather than getting defensive, she asked why nobody had raised the issue sooner. That question stung, because the honest answer was that we had assumed she wouldn't want to hear it. We had been reading her silence as approval, when in fact she simply hadn't had the full picture.

The lesson I took away is that upward feedback is less about courage than about preparation. A vague complaint puts your manager on the defensive; a concrete example with numbers gives them something to act on. And if you frame it as a way to protect a shared goal, rather than as a criticism of their judgment, most reasonable managers will hear you out.

questions.q: Why had the team stayed quiet about the deadline?
options: They believed Helen did not want to hear objections.
They thought the deadline was realistic.
Helen had told them not to criticize the plan.
A teammate had advised them to wait until June.
questions.explain_zh: 第 4 段：「we had assumed she wouldn't want to hear it」，大家以為 Helen 不想聽反對意見，所以沒人開口。

questions.q: What did the writer bring to the meeting with Helen?
options: A list of complaints from the team
An example, supporting data and a proposal
A new launch plan Helen had written
A request to hire more testers
questions.explain_zh: 第 2 段：「a specific example, the data behind it, and a proposal」。

questions.q: What does the writer imply about vague complaints?
options: They are the fastest way to get results.
They can make a manager defensive without giving them a clear next step.
Most managers prefer them to hard data.
They work best with senior managers.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。最後一段說含糊的抱怨會讓主管 on the defensive（處於守勢），而具體例子加數字才 gives them something to act on，暗示含糊的抱怨沒有給主管可以行動的方向。

listening.title: Peer Feedback After a Presentation

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Lena
lines.text: Got a sec? I wanted to give you some thoughts on this morning's presentation, if that's okay.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Raj
lines.text: Sure, go for it. Honestly, I could tell something was off halfway through.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Lena
lines.text: No, no, the content was solid. It's more the... how do I put this... the pacing. By the time you got to the budget slide, half the room had already checked out.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Raj
lines.text: Ugh, really? I'd rehearsed it, like, five times—

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Lena
lines.text: And it showed! You knew your stuff. But you spent almost twenty minutes on background that most people had already seen in the pre-read.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Raj
lines.text: Right. So I was basically repeating the deck they'd already gone through.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Lena
lines.text: Pretty much. If I were you, I'd open with the ask—the budget—and only fill in the background if people push back.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Raj
lines.text: Lead with the conclusion. Okay, that makes sense. Anything else?

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Lena
lines.text: Just one small thing. When Marco challenged the numbers, you sort of... brushed him off.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Raj
lines.text: Did I? I mean, I'd been expecting that question, so I guess I answered a bit too quickly.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Lena
lines.text: Yeah, it came across as a little dismissive. Next time, maybe just acknowledge his point before you answer.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Raj
lines.text: Fair enough. Thanks, Lena. I'd much rather hear it from you than in my review.

questions.q: What does Lena mean when she says "half the room had already checked out"?
options: Half the people had left the room.
Half the people had stopped paying attention.
Half the people had approved the budget.
Half the people had read the slides.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。check out 在這裡是「心思飄走、不再專心」，配合她在講節奏（pacing）太慢，可知是大家已經失去注意力。

questions.q: What does Lena suggest Raj do next time?
options: Rehearse fewer times
Start with the budget request
Skip the budget slide
Send the pre-read after the meeting
questions.explain_zh: Lena 說：「I'd open with the ask, the budget」，建議一開始就提出預算需求。

questions.q: How does Raj feel about the feedback by the end?
options: Annoyed
Grateful
Confused
Defensive
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。最後他說「Thanks, Lena. I'd much rather hear it from you than in my review.」，表示他很感謝能先從同事口中聽到。

dictation: So I was basically repeating the deck they'd already gone through.
I'd much rather hear it from you than in my review.

glossary.definition: how confident and positive a group of people feel
to gently encourage someone to do something
in a position where you feel you must defend yourself or your actions
to stop paying attention, especially because you are bored
to refuse to listen to someone or treat what they say as unimportant
showing that you think something is not worth considering
